mmaths-2020-mixer-01.title: Solution
mmaths-2020-mixer-01.body:
Choose the two boys who pair with each other: $\binom52=10$ ways. Choose the two girls who pair with each other: $\binom52=10$ ways. The remaining $3$ boys are matched with the remaining $3$ girls in $3!=6$ ways. Total $10\cdot10\cdot6=600$.

**Answer: 600**

mmaths-2020-mixer-02.title: Solution
mmaths-2020-mixer-02.body:
The product needs $2^5$. The single digits have $2$-adic valuations $2\to1$, $4\to2$, $6\to1$, $8\to3$, others $0$. A triple needs total valuation at least $5$ and sum at least $20$. The only triple of distinct digits with sum $\ge20$ and valuation $\ge5$ is $\{4,8,9\}$ (check: with $8$ and $4$ the third digit must be $9$ for the sum; triples such as $\{8,6,2\}$, $\{8,6,4\}$, $\{8,7,4\}$, $\{8,2,\cdot\}$ have sum below $20$). Britta's sum is $1+2+3+5+6+7=24$.

**Answer: 24**

mmaths-2020-mixer-03.title: Solution
mmaths-2020-mixer-03.body:
Ant$_1$ can stand at any of the $8$ vertices. The unvisited vertices must always form one contiguous arc of the octagon: if a next ant skipped a vertex, that vertex would be cut off by the chord just drawn and could not be reached later without crossing it (unless it were the very last vertex, which is the same as taking the end of the arc). So each ant from Ant$_2$ to Ant$_7$ chooses one of the two ends of the remaining arc ($2$ choices), and Ant$_8$ is forced. Total $8\cdot2^6=512$. (A brute-force check over all $8!$ placements also gives $512$.)

**Answer: 512**

mmaths-2020-mixer-04.title: Solution
mmaths-2020-mixer-04.body:
Claire leaves together with exactly one other person, equally likely any of the other $11$, so she leaves at the same time as Cat with probability $\frac1{11}$. Otherwise (probability $\frac{10}{11}$) they leave at different times, and by symmetry each is equally likely to go first. So $P(\text{Claire strictly first})=\frac{10}{11}\cdot\frac12=\frac5{11}$, and $a+b=5+11=16$.

**Answer: 16**

mmaths-2020-mixer-05.title: Solution
mmaths-2020-mixer-05.body:
Here $a,b\ne0$. Multiply by $ab$: $ab(a+b-2)=a(a+1)+b(b+1)=a^2+b^2+a+b$. Let $s=a+b$, $p=ab$: $p(s-2)=s^2-2p+s$, so $ps=s(s+1)$. Since $s\ne0$, $p=s+1$, i.e. $ab=a+b+1$, i.e. $(a-1)(b-1)=2$. The integer solutions are $(a-1,b-1)\in\{(1,2),(2,1),(-1,-2),(-2,-1)\}$, giving $(a,b)=(2,3),(3,2),(0,-1),(-1,0)$. The last two have a zero denominator. So $a\in\{2,3\}$ and the sum is $5$.

**Answer: 5**

mmaths-2020-mixer-06.title: Solution
mmaths-2020-mixer-06.body:
Let $\Omega$ have radius $R=1$ and let $s=AB=AC$. The circle centered at $A$ through $B,C$ has radius $s$ and meets line $AO$ at distance $s$ from $A$, at distance $s-1$ from $O$. By symmetry the tangency point of $\omega$ with this arc is on line $AO$, so $r=s-1$.

The distance from $O$ to chord $AB$ is $\sqrt{1-s^2/4}$ and this must equal $r$. So $(s-1)^2=1-\frac{s^2}{4}$, i.e. $\frac54s^2-2s=0$, $s=\frac85$, $r=\frac35$. The area ratio is $r^2=\frac9{25}$, so $a+b=9+25=34$.

**Answer: 34**

mmaths-2020-mixer-08.title: Solution
mmaths-2020-mixer-08.body:
Cases by the attack structure:

- Three rooks in one line (they give $2$ attacking pairs, the outer two being blocked by the middle one): $8$ lines, $\binom43$ choices of three cells, and the fourth rook must avoid that line and the three columns (or rows), leaving $3$ cells: $8\cdot4\cdot3=96$.
- An "L": a corner rook ($16$ choices), one rook in its row ($3$) and one in its column ($3$); the fourth rook must avoid the two rows and two columns used, leaving $4$ cells: $16\cdot9\cdot4=576$.
- Two disjoint pairs in columns: choose the two columns ($6$), the rows of the first pair ($6$), and the second pair uses the other two rows ($1$): $36$; the same for rows: $36$. Total $72$.
- One pair in a row and one pair in a column: choose the intersection cell of the row and column ($16$); the row pair uses two of the other $3$ cells of the row ($3$ ways), the column pair two of the other $3$ cells of the column ($3$ ways): $16\cdot9=144$.

Total $96+576+72+144=888$. (Brute force over all $\binom{16}{4}$ placements agrees.)

**Answer: 888**

mmaths-2020-mixer-09.title: Solution
mmaths-2020-mixer-09.body:
Let $BC=1$. For $DE=1$ with $BD=CE=\frac13$, $D$ lies on segment $BC$ and $E$ lies on the extension beyond $C$ (or the mirror image). Let $H$ be the foot of the altitude from $A$: $AH=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$, $HD=\frac16$, $HE=\frac56$. Then $AD=\sqrt{\frac34+\frac1{36}}=\frac{\sqrt{7}}{3}$ and $AE=\sqrt{\frac34+\frac{25}{36}}=\frac{\sqrt{13}}{3}$.

Computing $[ADE]$ two ways: $\frac12AD\cdot AE\sin\angle DAE=\frac12\,AH\cdot DE$, so $\sin\angle DAE=\frac{AH\cdot DE}{AD\cdot AE}=\frac{\sqrt3/2}{\sqrt{91}/9}=\frac{9\sqrt3}{2\sqrt{91}}=\frac{9\sqrt{273}}{182}$. Thus $a+b+c=9+273+182=464$ ($273=3\cdot7\cdot13$ is squarefree).

**Answer: 464**

mmaths-2020-mixer-10.title: Solution
mmaths-2020-mixer-10.body:
Write $\frac{na}{n+a}=n-\frac{n^2}{n+a}$. It is an integer iff $n+a$ divides $n^2$, and $n+a>n$. So $f(n)$ is the number of divisors of $n^2$ greater than $n$, which is $\frac{\tau(n^2)-1}{2}$.

For $n=3\cdot2^k$: $n^2=3^2\cdot2^{2k}$, $\tau=3(2k+1)$, so $f(3\cdot2^k)=\frac{6k+3-1}{2}=3k+1$. Then
$$A=\sum_{k=0}^{673}(3k+1)=3\cdot\frac{673\cdot674}{2}+674=2019\cdot337+674\equiv-337+674=337\pmod{2020}.$$

**Answer: 337**

mmaths-2020-mixer-11.title: Solution
mmaths-2020-mixer-11.body:
Let $u=\sqrt[3]a$ and $v=-\sqrt[3]b$, so $u+v=10$, $a=u^3$, $b=-v^3$ and $a-b=u^3+v^3$. Taking the real cube root of the second equation: $-uv=\frac{8-u^3+v^3}{6}$, i.e. $u^3-v^3=8+6uv$. Let $t=u-v$. Then $uv=\frac{100-t^2}{4}$ and $u^2+uv+v^2=\frac{300+t^2}{4}$, so $t\cdot\frac{300+t^2}{4}=8+\frac{6(100-t^2)}{4}$, i.e. $t^3+6t^2+300t-632=0$. It has the real root $t=2$ and $(t-2)(t^2+8t+316)=0$ where the quadratic factor has no real roots. So $u=6$, $v=4$, hence $a=216$, $b=-64$ and $a-b=280$.

Check: $\sqrt[3]{216}-\sqrt[3]{-64}=6+4=10$ and $ab=-13824$ while $\left(\frac{8-216+64}{6}\right)^3=(-24)^3=-13824$ ✓.

**Answer: 280**

mmaths-2020-mixer-12.title: Solution
mmaths-2020-mixer-12.body:
Since $f(d)-f(n)=(d-n)(d+n+1)$, $f(n)\mid f(d)$ iff $f(n)\mid(d-n)(d+n+1)$. Note $d=(n+1)^2$ always works: $d-n=f(n)$; this is the best possible when $f(n)$ is prime (or when the two factors share every prime of $f(n)$). A smaller $d$ exists only if the prime factors of $f(n)$ can be split between $d-n$ and $d+n+1$ (the two factors differ by $2n+1$).

- $n=6$: $f=43$ is prime, so $d\equiv6$ or $d\equiv36\pmod{43}$; $6,36$ are not coprime to $6$, so $d=49$.
- $n=7$: $f=57=3\cdot19$; the two factors differ by $15$, so $3$ divides both or neither; one needs $d\equiv1\pmod3$ and $d\equiv7$ or $11\pmod{19}$. $d=7,49$ fail coprimality, the next is $d=64$.
- $n=8$: $f=73$ is prime; $d\equiv8,64\pmod{73}$ are not coprime to $8$, so $d=81$.
- $n=9$: $f=91=7\cdot13$; take $d-9=7$ and $d+10=26$, so $d=16$ ($f(16)=273=3\cdot91$), and nothing smaller works.
- $n=10$: $f=111=3\cdot37$; the factors differ by $21$, so $3$ divides both, so again $d=(n+1)^2=121$.

Sum: $49+64+81+16+121=331$. (A computer search confirms these values.)

**Answer: 331**

mmaths-2020-mixer-13.title: Solution
mmaths-2020-mixer-13.body:
The line $MN$ is the midline parallel to $BC$, halfway between $A$ and $BC$, so the reflection of $D$ in $MN$ is $A$. Reflection in $MN$ preserves distances, so $AY=DX$. This is largest when $DX$ is a diameter, i.e. $X$ is the antipode of $D$ on circle $DMN$.

Coordinates: $B=(0,0)$, $C=(14,0)$, $A=(5,12)$, $D=(5,0)$, $M=(\frac52,6)$, $N=(\frac{19}{2},6)$. The center $O$ of circle $DMN$ lies on the perpendicular bisector $x=6$ of $MN$: $O=(6,y)$ with $OD^2=OM^2$: $1+y^2=\frac{49}{4}+(6-y)^2$, so $y=\frac{63}{16}$. The antipode of $D$ is $X=2O-D=\left(7,\frac{63}{8}\right)$. Then $AX^2=2^2+\left(12-\frac{63}{8}\right)^2=4+\frac{1089}{64}=\frac{1345}{64}$, so $AX=\frac{\sqrt{1345}}{8}$ ($1345=5\cdot269$ is squarefree) and $a+b=1345+8=1353$.

**Answer: 1353**

mmaths-2020-mixer-14.title: Solution
mmaths-2020-mixer-14.body:
Let $a=x+y$, $b=xy$, $c=(x-y)^2=a^2-4b>0$. Then the expression is $a^2+\frac{54}{bc}=c+4b+\frac{54}{bc}$. By AM-GM on the three terms $c$, $4b$, $\frac{54}{bc}$: $\ge3\sqrt[3]{c\cdot4b\cdot\frac{54}{bc}}=3\sqrt[3]{216}=18$. Equality needs $c=4b=\frac{54}{bc}=6$, i.e. $c=6$, $b=\frac32$, $a^2=c+4b=12$; then $x,y$ are the roots of $t^2-2\sqrt3\,t+\frac32=0$, which are distinct positive reals. So the minimum is $18$.

**Answer: 18**

mmaths-2020-mixer-15.title: Solution
mmaths-2020-mixer-15.body:
$f$ is the "logarithmic derivative" function: by induction, for $n=p_1^{a_1}\cdots p_r^{a_r}$, $f(n)=n\sum_{i}\frac{a_i}{p_i}$ (and $f(1)=0$). So $f(n)=n$ iff $\sum_i\frac{a_i}{p_i}=1$. Multiply by $P=p_1\cdots p_r$: modulo $p_j$ this gives $a_jP/p_j\equiv0$, so $p_j\mid a_j$ and $\frac{a_j}{p_j}\ge1$ for each $j$. The sum equals $1$ only if $r=1$ and $a_1=p_1$. So $n=p^p$ for a prime $p$.

We need $p^p<5^{50}=25^{25}$, i.e. $p<25$: $p=2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19,23$, which is $9$ values.

**Answer: 9**
